# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v3 (board-approved 17 Sep 2026)

## 1. Core frame
America wins the AI race on innovation and compute buildout. A patchwork of 50 state regimes raises costs, slows deployment and advantages the largest incumbents. ACIA supports one clear federal standard that regulates demonstrated harms, not speculative ones.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT. Ask that it be made permanent (or at minimum extended with a clean federal standard in place before sunset).
- Incident reporting: OPPOSE AS DRAFTED. Ask for a narrow definition of "critical safety incident", a 15-day window (match SB 53, not RAISE's 72 hours), confidentiality and FOIA exemption, and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters.
- CAISI: SUPPORT voluntary standards role; OPPOSE any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority. No position on the dollar figure.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "patchwork", "one national standard", "compliance costs fall hardest on startups", "light-touch, risk-based", "speculative risks".
- Catastrophic-risk scenarios: speculative, and not a sound basis for legislation. Keep the focus on costs and competitiveness.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# ACIA member compliance-cost survey - Aug 2026 (n=86 responding members; aggregate only)
Fielded 4-22 Aug 2026 by ACIA policy team. Not a probability sample.

| Item | Median | IQR |
|---|---|---|
| Est. annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework (developers >$500M revenue, n=11) | $1.4M | $0.8-2.6M |
| Est. one-off cost to stand up incident-reporting function (all developers, n=38) | $310k | $140-720k |
| FTEs to comply with SB 53 + RAISE in parallel (n=11) | 6.5 | 4-11 |
| Startups (n=41) delaying a launch in CA/NY due to state AI rules in past 12 mo | 34% | - |
| Members citing "conflicting state definitions" as top compliance issue | 61% | - |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?

# ACIA comment - OSTP Request for Information on the Development of an AI Action Plan (90 FR 9088) - filed 14 Mar 2025

To the Office of Science and Technology Policy (via ostp-ai-rfi@nitrd.gov):

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance appreciates the opportunity to respond... Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads...

1. Preempt the patchwork. ...
2. Unlock energy and compute. ...
3. Keep standards voluntary and industry-led. ...

Respectfully, Grant Holloway, President & CEO

Bipartisan AI draft proposes three-year preemption of state laws – Roll Call 

 Skip to content

 Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., teamed up with Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif. on the draft bill. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo) 

 By 
 Allison Mollenkamp 

 Posted June 4, 2026 at 5:08pm 

 Another artificial intelligence regulation framework has joined the growing ranks on Capitol Hill, this time focused primarily on model safety and workforce impacts.

 Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., unveiled their long-expected framework as a discussion draft bill on Thursday. Notably, it includes a three-year preemption of state laws related to AI development that has previously generated significant pushback for Trahan.

 Reps. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va.; Scott Franklin, R-Fla.; Scott Peters, D-Calif.; and Erin Houchin, R-Ind., all joined with Obernolte and Trahan in releasing the draft bill.

 The 269-page text , dubbed The Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, comes just days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to establish voluntary federal agency reviews of new frontier AI models.

 [Related:  Executive order sets voluntary cyber reviews for advanced AI ] 

 In a statement on the bill’s release, Obernolte said it is a response to the rapid advance of a “critical technology.”

 “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI,” he said. “We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.”

 Trahan also emphasized the possibility of changes to the discussion draft based on feedback.

 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” Trahan said.

 The bill would also extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035. That law allows companies to share cyber threat information without incurring antitrust liability. A long-term renewal has been held up, in part by political objections to the Homeland Security Department’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

 Preemption pushback

 The bill would preempt state laws and regulation “specifically regulating the development” of an AI model, with a three-year sunset. The bill specifies that preemption would not apply to laws related to the use or deployment of AI models. 

 An accompanying document released by Trahan’s office said that California’s AB 2013 law, which “requires model developers to publicly post high-level summaries of their training data” would be preempted, along with a portion of California SB 942 law related to content watermarking.

 It also called out frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois, saying they would be “federalized” under the bill, though the bill does not make a distinction between “federalization” and “preemption.”

 Unpacking the Great American AI Act
 Key provisions on AI transparency, audits, and federal preemption Written by : Tony Samp Danny Tobey Ashley Carr Alicia Smith Michael Atleson On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence (AI) legislation titled the “Great American AI Act” (GAAIA). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint op-ed in Bloomberg Law .

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and preemption: “Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough.”

 AI’s impact on the workforce: “Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.”

 US leadership internationally: “By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.”

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I)

 Workforce (Title II)

 Cybersecurity (Title III)

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV)

 Transparency in frontier AI models 

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (Section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (Section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (Section 113).

 Section 111 

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a “frontier AI framework” focused on risk mitigation and the handling of “catastrophic risk.” All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any “critical safety incidents” to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation (CAISI).

 Section 112 

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee “independent verification organizations (IVOs)” that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform “audits and assessments.”

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s “frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks.”

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General (AG) and state AGs. Such referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both Sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113 

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding “AI violations.” This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations “related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence.”

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills 

 All three sections borrow heavily from recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is thus the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another recently enacted state law in Virginia focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable preemption provisions 

 Title I of the bill would preempt state laws and rules “specifically regulating the development of” any AI model, where “development” is broadly defined as “acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment.” The bill explains that the purpose of such preemption is to allow the federal government to “establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks.” Such preemption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or preempt state laws or rules of "general applicability." Thus, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating companion bots  and commercial chatbot interactions .

 However, the preemption language could preempt several state laws imposing obligations on developers, including the three frontier developer laws described above.

 GAAIA incorporates multiple bipartisan bills 

 The draft text incorporates provisions from several bipartisan bills on AI policy addressing a variety of issues, including cybersecurity, AI education and workforce, fraud deterrence, whistleblower protections, data center energy efficiencies, and others.

 For instance, the draft bill incorporates text from a longstanding bipartisan measure, the Future of Artificial Intelligence Innovation Act of 2026, th

Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 FILTER 

 June 9, 2026 

 Share on Facebook

 Share on LinkedIn

 Share on Twitter

 Share on Google+
 -->

 Share through Email

 Justine Gluck 
 Policy Analyst, AI Policy and Legislation 

 About Justine 

 Blogs by Justine 

 Introduction 

 It has been an unusually active few weeks for AI safety policy. Following a new frontier model safety bill passed in Illinois , and a White House executive order on AI security, Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a bipartisan discussion draft for the Great American AI Act of 2026, adding another major federal proposal to the rapidly developing frontier AI landscape.

 The draft is broad, covering issues ranging from workforce development and AI literacy to cybersecurity and international standards. But for many AI developers and deployers, the most important provisions are those focused on frontier model regulation. The draft would create requirements related to frontier AI transparency, critical safety incident reporting, employee whistleblower protections, and independent verification organizations. It would also include a three-year preemption clause restricting state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 This blog highlights four key takeaways of the discussion draft: 

 The draft is one of the first bipartisan attempts in Congress to address both frontier model safety and preemption of AI. These aspects make it a notable legislative effort, even if its prospects are uncertain. 

 The draft incorporates many of the frontier model safety provisions in existing state laws but also has key distinctions. Compared to recent state frontier AI laws in California , New York , and Illinois (pending signature), the bill makes some important adjustments, like adding a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” modifying the definition of “critical safety incident,” and utilizing a different penalty structure. 

 The draft brings the preemption debate back into the federal AI policy conversation . It includes a three-year preemption clause focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. 

 The draft also reaches beyond frontier model safety. Other notable provisions include a study content moderation, a federal voluntary model testing program, and disclosure requirements for AI-related mass layoffs.

 The Act Enters the AI Safety and Preemption Debate  

 Amidst a crowded but unsettled federal AI policy landscape, the Great American AI Act is notable for its regulatory focus, bipartisan backing, and what it may signal for federal AI governance ahead. Though Congress has introduced no shortage of AI bills, there has been limited movement toward enacted legislation. Congress has considered sector-specific bills on chatbots 1 , regulatory sandboxes , defense , elections , and financial scams , as well as broader proposals aimed at establishing a national AI framework like Sen. Blackburn’s (R-TN) TRUMP AMERICA AI Act .

 Amid this activity, the Great American AI Act steps into two of the most active and contested AI policy debates: frontier model safety and federal preemption. On AI safety, the draft follows a period of growing attention to frontier model oversight at both the state and federal levels, where policymakers are trying to balance concerns about catastrophic risks and national security with concerns that overly burdensome requirements could slow AI innovation or weaken U.S. competitiveness.

 On preemption, the draft arrives less than a year after Congress rejected a much broader effort to pause state AI regulation. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to remove a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. By contrast, the Great American AI Act includes a narrower three-year preemption provision focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 The draft is also significant because of both who introduced it and how they introduced it. Other federal AI bills have addressed AI safety or included preemption language, but this proposal comes from bipartisan sponsors who have been closely involved in federal AI policy 2 . In introducing the draft, the sponsors emphasized that “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.” Just as importantly, they have framed the draft as a starting point rather than a final product, describing it as “the start of a serious national conversation.” Whether the bill advances in its current form remains uncertain, especially given the sensitivity of federal preemption and the range of issues addressed. Even if the draft changes, it may help shape the terms of future federal debates over AI safety. At a minimum, it is another sign that Congress is increasingly focused on how to govern AI systems and how federal rules should interact with the fast-moving state AI landscape.

 Frontier AI Requirements: Where the Draft Aligns with State Laws 

 The draft’s frontier model provisions are not starting from scratch. They closely track the framework emerging from California’s SB 53 , New York’s RAISE Act , and Illinois’ SB 315 (awaiting signature), including requirements for frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, safety incident reporting, enforcement, and whistleblower protections. But the federal draft makes some important adjustments, including a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” a definition of “critical safety incident” that is broader in some respects and narrower in others, and a federal enforcement structure with penalties of up to $1 million per day.

 Key Definitions 

 The Draft largely aligns with recent state frontier AI laws’ definitions of “large frontier developer,” “frontier model” (encompassing foundation models trained using more than 10^26 computational operations), and “catastrophic risk” (covering certain risks of death, serious injury, or major property damage arising from frontier models). For more background on SB 53 and the RAISE Act, see FPF’s prior analysis . There are, however, a few notable differences. 

 First, unlike the state laws, the Draft requires “frontier developers” to have a gross revenue exceeding $50 million. The state laws only include a gross revenue qualifier in the definition of “large frontier developer.”

 Second, the draft’s definition of “catastrophic risk” does not  specify that the death, serious injury, or property damage must arise from a “single incident,” as in the state laws.

 Finally, the draft’s definition of “critical safety incident” differs from the state laws by not mandating actual harm occur (such as death, bodily injury, or property loss), nor does it include scenarios where the model uses deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring.

Obernolte, Trahan Introduce Bipartisan FRONTIER Act to Strengthen Oversight of Advanced AI | Representative Jay Obernolte

 2433 Rayburn House Office Building, Washington, DC 20515 Email Me 202-225-5861

 Image 

 Obernolte, Trahan Introduce Bipartisan FRONTIER Act to Strengthen Oversight of Advanced AI 

 Image July 23, 2026 Press Release WASHINGTON, D.C. —  Today, Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Congresswomen Lori Trahan (D-MA), alongside Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Scott Peters (D-CA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Suhas Subramanyan (D-VA),  introduced the Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act, or the FRONTIER Act. The bipartisan legislation, which was developed as part of the broader Great American AI Act framework, establishes a national, risk-based framework governing the development and deployment of the most advanced artificial intelligence models.  
 The FRONTIER Act establishes tiered requirements based on the size of a frontier AI developer, including model cards, risk-management frameworks, independent audits, incident reporting, and ongoing assessments. It also creates a uniform national standard for transparency, auditing, and reporting of catastrophic risk to prevent a patchwork of state regulations.  
 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, and Congress must ensure our regulatory framework keeps pace without undermining American innovation,” said Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23). “The FRONTIER Act focuses oversight on the largest developers and most advanced models, requiring transparency, independent evaluation, and timely reporting of serious safety incidents. This legislation will protect Americans from catastrophic risk, provide developers with clear rules of the road, and ensure the United States remains the global leader in AI.” 
 “As AI systems grow more capable, Americans deserve confidence that the most powerful models are being developed responsibly,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03). “The bipartisan FRONTIER Act delivers commonsense transparency and independent oversight for the largest AI developers while giving them a single, clear national standard to build on. This is how we protect the public from catastrophic risks without slowing the innovation that keeps America competitive.” 
 "The FRONTIER Act recognizes that not every AI developer should be regulated the same way. It takes a targeted approach by focusing only on the handful of companies developing the most powerful frontier AI models, not the startups and innovators driving America's AI ecosystem,” said Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18). “By tying coverage to substantial AI research and development investments and requiring transparency and independent assessments from those developers, the bill avoids one-size-fits-all mandates and allows smaller innovators to spend their time building new technologies instead of navigating unnecessary federal red tape." 
 "The window to get AI policy right is closing, and Congress can't afford to miss it," said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). "I supported Representatives Trahan and Obernolte's initial draft so we could develop a better bill that reflects how this technology works and where it's headed. Thanks to input from researchers, experts, and civil society advocates, that process worked. The FRONTIER Act is a targeted bill with clear, uniform transparency, and safety standards, instead of a fifty-state patchwork. I'm glad to support this bipartisan effort so that Congress acts before this technology outruns us." 
 "America must lead the world in artificial intelligence, and we can do that while being clear-eyed about the risks,” said Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09). “Just this week, one of the most advanced AI systems in the country broke out of its own developer's testing environment, reaching systems it was never supposed to touch. This is exactly the kind of incident that shouldn't stay behind closed doors. The FRONTIER Act delivers transparency and accountability from the largest AI developers. Innovation and guardrails are not opposites—both are necessary to stay ahead of our adversaries." 
 "This is a four-alarm fire. We need to take action now. These frontier models could have the power to create serious chaos and harm without adequate regulations,” said Congressman Subramanyan (VA-10). “This bill, while not perfect, is an important, bipartisan step in the right direction. We need a bill like this that can actually pass this Congress and get signed into law. But this is only the first step, and more action needs to be taken to protect people from the harm these models can cause." 
 Read the bill here . 
 Read the section by section of the bill here .

 Answered from the bill text, with the section cited. Ask your own above.
 Who does the Great American AI Act regulate?
 Based on the discussion draft sections provided, the Act targets several distinct groups:
 Frontier Developers 
 Entities that have trained a frontier model (a foundation model trained using more than 10²⁶ computing operations) AND had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior year (Sec. 101)
 A subset called "large frontier developers" must have had more than $500 million in gross revenue (Sec. 101)
 AI Developers More Broadly 
 Any person or entity that determines training objectives and performs or directs training, fine-tuning, or substantial modification of an AI model prior to deployment (Sec. 121)
 State-level regulation of these developers' pre-deployment activities is preempted by federal law — at least for 3 years after enactment (Sec. 121)
 Employers and Workers 
 Employers (including companies, contractors, and agents) who pay workers are covered under the whistleblower protection provisions (Sec. 113)
 "Covered individuals" include current and former employees and independent contractors (Sec. 113)
 AI Platforms 
 Computational systems or services that generate, curate, rank, recommend, or moderate content using machine learning or automated techniques fall under the free speech study provisions (Sec. 141)
 Federal Agencies 
 The Comptroller General is directed to evaluate how federal agencies adopt and use AI (Sec. 122)
 Federal agency interactions with AI platforms regarding content and speech are subject to study (Sec. 141)
 ---
 Keep in mind this is a discussion draft dated 2026-06-02, and the scope of who is regulated may change. For questions about a specific organization's obligations, consult qualified legal counsel.
 Sec. 122 Sec. 113 Sec. 121 Sec. 141 Sec. 101 What must large frontier developers disclose before deploying a new model?
 Before deploying a new frontier model (or one with a substantial modification), here is what the draft requires to be published on a publicly available website:
 From Sec. 111(c), a transparency report must include:
 A mechanism for individuals to contact the developer
 The model's release date
 Each language the model supports (if any)
 Each output modality (e.g., text, image, audio)
 The intended use of the model
 Any restrictions or conditions on use
 Each catastrophic risk assessment conducted under the developer's frontier AI framework
 The results of each such assessment
 The extent to which a third party was involved in the risk assessment
 Any other steps taken under the framework with respect to that model
 Additionally, under Sec. 111(a), large frontier developers (those with over $500 million in gross revenue — see Sec. 101(15)) must already have a frontier AI framework published that covers how they identify risk thresholds, assess catastrophic risk, use third-party evaluators, handle cybersecurity of model weights, and more.
 A few things to keep in mind:
 Developers may redact certain information to protect trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety, or national security — but must include a note explaining the character of any redaction (Sec. 111(e)).
 Knowingly making inaccurate or misleading statements in the transparency report is prohibited, with a good-faith exception (Sec. 111(d)).
 This is a discussion draft dated 2026-06-02, so these provisions may change.
 For questions about how these requirements apply to a specific organization, consulting qualified legal counsel is advisable.
 Sec. 111 Sec. 101 What is a large frontier developer under the bill?
 Under the draft bill, a "large frontier developer" is defined in Sec. 101 as a frontier developer that, in the calendar year immediately before the year at issue, had more than $500,000,000 in gross revenue — counting revenue collectively with every affiliate of that developer.
 To break that down, it builds on two earlier definitions:
 A "frontier developer" is an entity that has trained (or initiated the training of) a frontier model AND had more than $50,000,000 in gross revenue (with affiliates) in the preceding calendar year. (Sec. 101)
 A "frontier model" is a foundation model trained using more than 10²⁶ integer or floating-point operations, including the original training run and any subsequent fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or other substantial modification the developer applies to it. (Sec. 101)
 So, in plain terms, a large frontier developer is a company (or similar entity) that:
 1. Has trained a very large AI model (above the 10²⁶ compute threshold), and
 2. Brought in more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior year, counting affiliated entities together.
 This distinction matters because the draft imposes the most significant obligations — such as publishing a frontier AI framework (Sec. 111) and undergoing semi-annual independent audits (Sec. 112) — specifically on large frontier developers.

{"path": "/workspace/out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md", "content": "DRAFT FOR PRESIDENT & CEO SIGN-OFF - Friday, Oct. 23, 2026
Work order ACIA-POL-2026-117. Internal header to be stripped before transmission.

---

[ACIA letterhead]

October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 on June 4, and for keeping it open for stakeholder comment ahead of introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington, D.C. coalition of roughly 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads in this technology.

ACIA supports the draft's central design. One clear federal standard, in place of a 50-state patchwork, is the most pro-innovation step Congress can take on AI. As we wrote in our March 2025 comments to the Office of Science and Technology Policy on the AI Action Plan, the patchwork is not an abstraction for our members. It is a line item, and it is growing.

We write with five requests. Make the draft's preemption of state AI development laws permanent. Narrow the definition of "critical safety incident." Hold the 15-day incident reporting window, and add confidentiality protections and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters. Keep the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) on a voluntary footing, with no mandatory pre-deployment testing authority. And hold every obligation in the final text to a demonstrated-harm test rather than to speculative risk scenarios.

## 1. One national standard (Sec. 121): support, and make it permanent

Section 121 would displace state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while leaving untouched state laws on use and deployment, laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. That is the right line. Development is interstate commerce. A model trained in one state is used in all 50, and it is built once, not 50 times.

The alternative is already here, and it is expensive. California's SB 53 has been in effect since Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, as amended in March 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 and puts critical safety incidents on a 72-hour clock. Illinois' SB 315, signed July 6, 2026 and effective Jan. 1, 2028, adds the country's first mandatory third-party audit requirement. Three states, three definitions, three reporting windows, three audit regimes. Colorado, meanwhile, repealed and replaced its own 2024 AI law in May 2026, weeks before it was to take effect and after a federal court had blocked its enforcement. Companies cannot plan against rules that change underneath them.

Our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members, aggregate data only) puts numbers on this. Sixty-one percent of members rank conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem. Among startup members, 34 percent delayed a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Developers running parallel compliance programs report a median of 6.5 full-time employees on the task, with a median of $1.4 million a year to maintain a published frontier safety framework. Those are resources not spent on training runs, chips or customers.

Our request on Sec. 121 is simple: make preemption permanent. If a sunset is unavoidable, it should not take effect until the federal standard is fully operational, regulations issued, the CAISI reporting mechanism live and independent verification organizations licensed, and it should be measured from that date, not from enactment. A three-year clock that starts at enactment guarantees a relitigation in 2029 and tells compliance teams to build for the patchwork's return. We would also caution against narrowing proposals, including the one-to-one preemption approach under discussion elsewhere in the framework. A preemption clause that swaps one federal rule for one state rule is not a national standard.

## 2. Incident reporting (Secs. 101(7), 111): opposed as drafted, fixable with five changes

ACIA supports a single federal incident reporting channel. We oppose the incident reporting provisions of Section 111 as drafted, for one reason above all: the definition is too broad to be workable.

Under Sec. 101(7), a "critical safety incident" is any unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights; any failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures; or any "loss of control" of the model. There is no harm threshold. On that definition, a routine security event, a guardrail that misfires during internal testing, or an anomaly that turns out to be nothing becomes a reportable federal incident, on a statute that carries civil penalties of up to $1 million per day. Our members' survey shows a median one-off cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident reporting function, before the first report is ever filed.

We ask the sponsors to make five changes.

First, narrow the definition in Sec. 101(7) to incidents that cause, or credibly threaten in the near term, actual and material harm to people, property or critical systems. A reporting regime should capture what went wrong, not what a hypothetical might one day go wrong.

Second, hold the 15-day reporting window in Sec. 111(g), with the 24-hour trigger for imminent risk of death or serious injury. Fifteen days matches California's SB 53. It is enough time for a developer to establish facts and file an accurate report, which is what regulators actually need. We note that the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, introduced in July as the frontier-model title of this framework, would tighten the clock to 72 hours, as New York does. We ask the sponsors to hold the line at 15 days and not import the 72-hour standard into the final text.

Third, make confidentiality explicit. The draft exempts from disclosure under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3) the information developers share with CAISI in connection with the center's evaluation functions. We ask that the same exemption and non-disclosure protections expressly cover incident reports submitted under Secs. 111(f) and 111(g), including any sharing with attorneys general under the opt-in provision in Sec. 111(h). Incident reports will contain some of the most security-sensitive information a developer holds. If a report can become a public document, or a discovery exhibit, developers will write it defensively, and the government will learn less.

Fourth, add a safe harbor for good-faith reports. A developer that reports promptly and honestly should not face penalties, or follow-on litigation, on the theory that its initial filing was incomplete. Safe harbors are what produce candid reporting.

Fifth, fix the enforcement back door. Under Sec. 111(h), state attorneys general may opt in to receive reports, and may then bring actions for civil penalties and injunctions. One incident, reported once to one federal official, could be routed to as many state enforcers as opt in, each with its own theory of the case. That is the patchwork re-entering the building through a side door. State enforcement, if retained at all, should be a backstop that follows federal interpretations, with notice to the Department of Justice.

## 3. CAISI (Sec. 102): support codification, keep the mission voluntary

ACIA supports Sec. 102. Codifying CAISI within the Department of Commerce, under a Secretary-appointed Director, with a mandate to develop voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards for AI security, to evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress, and to support synthetic content detection, is sound policy. Today CAISI operates on roughly $15 million a year. A codified, stably funded CAISI is a better answer than 50 state analogues, and we support the direction of the draft.

Two guardrails, please. First, the final text should state expressly that CAISI's testing and evaluation of frontier systems is voluntary and conducted by agreement with developers, as the center's existing cooperative arrangements with leading developers already work. Any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority, or any federal gate on releasing a model, would be the most consequential expansion of federal control over the AI stack in the statute, and it would operate against speculative rather than demonstrated risk. We urge the sponsors to resist it in every title of the final framework.

Second, take care with fee authority. Sec. 102 authorizes the center to collect fees from independent verification organizations and large frontier developers. Fees of that kind pass straight back to industry, and compliance costs fall hardest on startups and small suppliers even when they are nominally aimed at the largest firms. Scope them narrowly and give the Government Accountability Office a regular look.

ACIA takes no position on the $100 million annual authorization level for fiscal 2027 through 2029.

## 4. Regulate demonstrated harms, not speculative scenarios

The draft is built around "catastrophic risk," defined in Sec. 101 as a foreseeable and material risk of death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage. ACIA's members plan against real failure modes every day: weight theft, data center outages, supply chain interruptions, energy constraints. They do not plan against science fiction, and neither should federal law.

Speculative catastrophe scenarios are not a sound basis for legislation. They cannot be audited, they cannot be priced, and they invite agencies to regulate capability rather than harm. The draft's own structure shows the right instinct: a high threshold, tiered obligations, and the heaviest requirements reserved for developers above $500 million in revenue. We ask the sponsors to keep it that way, and to add a discipline to the definitional machinery: if CAISI or the Secretary recommends updating key definitions in future years, those changes should go through notice-and-comment and be subject to congressional review, not take effect as a matter of agency discretion. A light-touch, risk-based framework stays light-touch only if its thresholds do not drift.

## 5. Provisions ACIA supports

Our members strongly support the parts of the draft that expand capacity rather than paperwork, including the GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation, including energy (Sec. 122); the AI testbed program at the Energy Department, NIST and NSF (Sec. 401); the codification of the National AI Research Resource; grants to maintainers of critical open-source software (Sec. 311); the GAO review of model weight, data center and open-source security (Sec. 321); international standards coalitions that keep American firms at the head of the table (Sec. 411); reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 (Sec. 301); and penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials (Sec. 132). These are practical, bipartisan and overdue.

## Conclusion

This draft is the closest Congress has come to answering the question our members ask most often: which law applies? On the core choice, one national standard versus 50 state ones, ACIA is with you. Fix the incident reporting definition, protect the 15-day window, keep CAISI voluntary, and make preemption permanent, and the introduced bill will have our active support.

We would welcome the chance to walk through these comments with your staff and with the Energy and Commerce Committee, and to connect your offices with technical experts from our membership. Please contact our policy team to schedule.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
Washington, D.C.
"}

{"content": "# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on ACIA's GAAIA comments

Work order ACIA-POL-2026-117. Answers for Hill and committee staff, each under 120 words. Positions per messaging guide v3; survey data cited in aggregate only.

## 1. If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53. (Majority E&C staff)

We support one federal reporting channel. That is the point of preemption. Our objection is the definition in Sec. 101(7): it has no harm threshold, so any weight access, any risk-mitigation failure or any "loss of control" becomes a reportable federal incident, with penalties up to $1 million per day. A broad definition makes the federal regime heavier than the state rules it replaces. Our survey shows a median $310,000 to stand up a reporting function and 6.5 staff running parallel regimes today. Narrow the definition to actual or imminent material harm, keep the 15-day window, add confidentiality and a safe harbor, and we can support it.

## 2. Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept? (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned)

Plenty, and most are already in the draft. Our largest members already publish frontier AI frameworks under state law. ACIA accepts published frameworks with annual review (Sec. 111(a)); pre-deployment transparency reports (Sec. 111(c)); a single, narrow, confidential federal incident reporting channel on the draft's 15-day window (Secs. 111(f)-(g)); third-party verification retained by developers above $500 million in revenue (Sec. 112); and whistleblower anti-retaliation (Sec. 113). What we cannot accept: obligations keyed to speculative capability scenarios, a federal pre-deployment release gate, and 50-state enforcement through the attorney general opt-in (Sec. 111(h)). Regulate demonstrated harms, not hypothetical ones, and we are with you.

## 3. Three years or permanent: what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset? (Senate Commerce staff)

Permanent. Development is interstate commerce, and a three-year clock guarantees a relitigation in 2029 while telling compliance teams to budget for the patchwork's return. Our members are making five-year compute and facility commitments now. If a sunset is needed to move the bill, we would ask for three things: a longer runway; a clock that starts when the federal standard is fully operational, meaning regulations issued, the CAISI reporting mechanism live and verification organizations licensed; and no lapse before the standard has demonstrably replaced state obligations. We also oppose one-to-one preemption. Swapping one federal rule for one state rule is not a national standard.

## 4. CAISI is authorized at $100M per year. What's your view on the funding level? (Appropriations staff)

ACIA takes no position on the dollar figure. Our members care what the money buys. CAISI operates on roughly $15 million a year today, and the sponsors' own FAQ describes $100 million as an order-of-magnitude increase. A stably funded, codified CAISI is far preferable to 50 state analogues, so we are comfortable with the direction. Two guardrails: keep the mission voluntary, meaning guidelines, standards and evaluation by agreement with developers, with no mandatory pre-deployment testing authority; and watch the fee authority on verification organizations and large frontier developers, which passes costs straight back to industry. Whatever the number, annual reporting on what the center delivers would help appropriators judge it.
", "path": "/workspace/out/staff_qa.md"}

DRAFT FOR PRESIDENT & CEO SIGN-OFF - Friday, Oct. 23, 2026
Work order ACIA-POL-2026-117. Internal header to be stripped before transmission.

---

[ACIA letterhead]

October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 on June 4, and for keeping it open for stakeholder comment ahead of introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington, D.C. coalition of roughly 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads in this technology.

ACIA supports the draft's central design. One clear federal standard, in place of a 50-state patchwork, is the most pro-innovation step Congress can take on AI. As we wrote in our March 2025 comments to the Office of Science and Technology Policy on the AI Action Plan, the patchwork is not an abstraction for our members. It is a line item, and it is growing.

We write with five requests. Make the draft's preemption of state AI development laws permanent. Narrow the definition of "critical safety incident." Hold the 15-day incident reporting window, and add confidentiality protections and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters. Keep the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) on a voluntary footing, with no mandatory pre-deployment testing authority. And hold every obligation in the final text to a demonstrated-harm test rather than to speculative risk scenarios.

## 1. One national standard (Sec. 121): support, and make it permanent

Section 121 would displace state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while leaving untouched state laws on use and deployment, laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. That is the right line. Development is interstate commerce. A model trained in one state is used in all 50, and it is built once, not 50 times.

The alternative is already here, and it is expensive. California's SB 53 has been in effect since Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, as amended in March 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 and puts critical safety incidents on a 72-hour clock. Illinois' SB 315, signed July 6, 2026 and effective Jan. 1, 2028, adds the country's first mandatory third-party audit requirement. Three states, three definitions, three reporting windows, three audit regimes. Colorado, meanwhile, repealed and replaced its own 2024 AI law in May 2026, weeks before it was to take effect and after a federal court had blocked its enforcement. Companies cannot plan against rules that change underneath them.

Our August 2026 member survey, 86 responding members, aggregate data only, not a probability sample, puts numbers on this. Sixty-one percent of members rank conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem. Among startup members, 34 percent delayed a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Our largest developers report a median of 6.5 full-time employees to comply with California and New York in parallel, and a median of $1.4 million a year to maintain a published frontier safety framework. Those are resources not spent on training runs, chips or customers.

Our request on Sec. 121 is simple: make preemption permanent. If a sunset is unavoidable, it should not take effect until the federal standard is fully operational, regulations issued, the CAISI reporting mechanism live and independent verification organizations licensed, and it should be measured from that date, not from enactment. A three-year clock that starts at enactment guarantees a relitigation in 2029 and tells compliance teams to build for the patchwork's return. We would also caution against narrowing proposals, including the one-to-one preemption approach under discussion elsewhere in the framework. A preemption clause that swaps one federal rule for one state rule is not a national standard.

## 2. Incident reporting (Secs. 101(7), 111): opposed as drafted, fixable with five changes

ACIA supports a single federal incident reporting channel. We oppose the incident reporting provisions of Section 111 as drafted, for one reason above all: the definition is too broad to be workable.

Under Sec. 101(7), a "critical safety incident" is any unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights; any failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures; or any "loss of control" of the model. There is no harm threshold. On that definition, a routine security event, a guardrail that misfires during internal testing, or an anomaly that turns out to be nothing becomes a reportable federal incident, on a statute that carries civil penalties of up to $1 million per day. Our members' survey shows a median one-off cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident reporting function, before the first report is ever filed.

We ask the sponsors to make five changes.

First, narrow the definition in Sec. 101(7) to incidents that cause, or credibly threaten in the near term, actual and material harm to people, property or critical systems. A reporting regime should capture what went wrong, not what a hypothetical might one day go wrong.

Second, hold the 15-day reporting window in Sec. 111(g), with the 24-hour trigger for imminent risk of death or serious injury. Fifteen days matches California's SB 53. It is enough time for a developer to establish facts and file an accurate report, which is what regulators actually need. We 
... [117 chars truncated] ...
k to 72 hours, as New York does. We ask the sponsors to hold the line at 15 days and not import the 72-hour standard into the final text.

Third, make confidentiality explicit. The draft exempts from disclosure under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3) the information developers share with CAISI in connection with the center's evaluation functions. We ask that the same exemption and non-disclosure protections expressly cover incident reports submitted under Secs. 111(f) and 111(g), including any sharing with attorneys general under the opt-in provision in Sec. 111(h). Incident reports will contain some of the most security-sensitive information a developer holds. If a report can become a public document, or a discovery exhibit, developers will write it defensively, and the government will learn less.

Fourth, add a safe harbor for good-faith reports. A developer that reports promptly and honestly should not face penalties, or follow-on litigation, on the theory that its initial filing was incomplete. Safe harbors are what produce candid reporting.

Fifth, fix the enforcement back door. Under Sec. 111(h), state attorneys general may opt in to receive reports, and may then bring actions for civil penalties and injunctions. One incident, reported once to one federal official, could be routed to as many state enforcers as opt in, each with its own theory of the case. That is the patchwork re-entering the building through a side door. State enforcement, if retained at all, should be a backstop that follows federal interpretations, with notice to the Department of Justice.

## 3. CAISI (Sec. 102): support codification, keep the mission voluntary

ACIA supports Sec. 102. Codifying CAISI within the Department of Commerce, under a Secretary-appointed Director, with a mandate to develop voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards for AI security, to evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress, and to support synthetic content detection, is sound policy. Today CAISI operates on roughly $15 million a year. A codified, stably funded CAISI is a better answer than 50 state analogues, and we support the direction of the draft.

Two guardrails, please. First, the final text should state expressly that CAISI's testing and evaluation of frontier systems is voluntary and conducted by agreement with developers, as the center's existing cooperative arrangements with leading developers already work. Any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority, or any federal gate on releasing a model, would be the most consequential expansion of federal control over the AI stack in the final bill, and it would operate against speculative rather than demonstrated risk. We urge the sponsors to resist it in every title of the framework.

Second, take care with fee authority. Sec. 102 authorizes the center to collect fees from independent verification organizations and large frontier developers. Fees of that kind pass straight back to industry, and compliance costs fall hardest on startups and small suppliers even when they are nominally aimed at the largest firms. Scope them narrowly and give the Government Accountability Office a regular look.

ACIA takes no position on the $100 million annual authorization level for fiscal 2027 through 2029.

## 4. Regulate demonstrated harms, not speculative scenarios

The draft is built around "catastrophic risk," defined in Sec. 101 as a foreseeable and material risk of death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage. ACIA's members plan against real failure modes every day: weight theft, data center outages, supply chain interruptions, energy constraints. They do not plan against science fiction, and neither should federal law.

Speculative catastrophe scenarios are not a sound basis for legislation. They cannot be audited, they cannot be priced, and they invite agencies to regulate capability rather than harm. The draft's own structure shows the right instinct: a high threshold, tiered obligations, and the heaviest requirements reserved for developers above $500 million in revenue. We ask the sponsors to keep it that way, and to add a discipline to the definitional machinery: if CAISI or the Secretary recommends updating key definitions in future years, those changes should go through notice-and-comment and be subject to congressional review, not take effect as a matter of agency discretion. A light-touch, risk-based framework stays light-touch only if its thresholds do not drift.

## 5. Provisions ACIA supports

Our members strongly support the parts of the draft that expand capacity rather than paperwork, including the GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation, including energy (Sec. 122); the AI testbed program at the Energy Department, NIST and NSF (Sec. 401); the codification of the National AI Research Resource; grants to maintainers of critical open-source software (Sec. 311); the GAO review of model weight, data center and open-source security (Sec. 321); international standards coalitions that keep American firms at the head of the table (Sec. 411); reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 (Sec. 301); and penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials (Sec. 132). These are practical, bipartisan and overdue.

## Conclusion

This draft is the closest Congress has come to answering the question our members ask most often: which law applies? On the core choice, one national standard versus 50 state ones, ACIA is with you. Fix the incident reporting definition, protect the 15-day window, keep CAISI voluntary, and make preemption permanent, and the introduced bill will have our active support.

We would welcome the chance to walk through these comments with your staff and with the Energy and Commerce Committee, and to connect your offices with technical experts from our membership. Please contact our policy team to schedule.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
Washington, D.C.

# One National AI Standard: Support GAAIA, Fix the Draft

**For Energy & Commerce member offices | ACIA | Oct. 2026**

**Who we are:** The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a Washington, D.C. coalition of about 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers behind U.S. AI leadership.

**Bottom line:** ACIA supports the discussion draft's central design. One clear federal standard beats a 50-state patchwork. We ask for five targeted changes before introduction.

## The problem: three states, three regimes

California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with 72-hour incident reporting. Illinois' SB 315, signed July 6, 2026, adds the first mandatory third-party audit, effective 2028. Colorado repealed and replaced its own 2024 AI law in May 2026, weeks before it was to take effect.

Our August 2026 survey of 86 members (aggregate data): 61% call conflicting state definitions their top compliance problem. 34% of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York this year. Parallel state compliance costs a median 6.5 full-time staff and $1.4 million a year at the largest developers.

## Five asks

1. **Make preemption permanent (Sec. 121).** Development is interstate commerce. At minimum, no sunset until the federal standard is fully operational, measured from that date, not enactment. Reject one-to-one preemption, which swaps one federal rule for one state rule.

2. **Narrow "critical safety incident" (Sec. 101(7)).** As drafted it has no harm threshold: any weight access, any guardrail failure, any "loss of control" is reportable, with penalties up to $1 million per day. Limit it to incidents causing or credibly threatening actual and material harm.

3. **Hold the 15-day reporting window (Sec. 111(g)).** It matches California. Do not import New York's 72-hour clock. Add express confidentiality and a 552(b)(3) FOIA exemption for incident reports, and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters.

4. **Keep CAISI voluntary (Sec. 102).** Support codification. Testing and evaluation should be by agreement with developers. No mandatory pre-deployment testing authority and no federal release gate. Watch the fee authority on auditors and large developers.

5. **Close the state enforcement back door (Sec. 111(h)).** The attorney general opt-in lets one report be routed to any number of state enforcers. State enforcement, if retained, should be a backstop that follows federal interpretations.

**Regulate demonstrated harms, not speculative scenarios.** Speculative catastrophe scenarios are not a sound basis for legislation. Keep the framework light-touch, risk-based and tied to real harms and real costs.

**Contact:** ACIA policy team, Washington, D.C.

# GAAIA discussion draft: ACIA asks by section

Work order ACIA-POL-2026-117. Positions per ACIA messaging guide v3 (board-approved Sept. 17, 2026). Section numbers cite the June 4, 2026 discussion draft.

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sec. 121. Federalization of state laws regulating AI model development (three-year preemption; use, deployment and general-applicability laws not preempted) | SUPPORT | Make preemption permanent; at minimum run any sunset from the date the federal standard is fully operational, not from enactment; reject one-to-one preemption | One national standard beats a 50-state patchwork, and a rule that expires invites the patchwork back. |
| Sec. 101(7). Definition of "critical safety incident" (any weight access, modification or exfiltration; any risk-mitigation failure; any "loss of control") | OPPOSE AS DRAFTED | Narrow to incidents that cause, or credibly threaten in the near term, actual and material harm | With no harm threshold, routine events become federal reports, and paperwork crowds out the signal. |
| Sec. 111(f)-(g). Confidential federal reporting mechanism; 15-day report (24 hours if imminent risk of death or serious injury) | SUPPORT THE TIMELINE, FIX THE SCOPE | Hold the 15-day window; do not import New York's 72-hour clock; apply the narrowed Sec. 101(7) definition | Fifteen days matches California SB 53 and gives developers time to file an accurate report. |
| Sec. 111(f)-(g). Confidentiality of incident reports | AMEND | Extend the draft's 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3) exemption and non-disclosure protections expressly to incident reports, including when shared under Sec. 111(h) | Security-sensitive reports that can become public or discoverable will be written defensively, and regulators learn less. |
| Sec. 111. Civil penalties, up to $1 million per day | AMEND | Add a safe harbor for good-faith reporters, proportional penalties, a cure period and a good-faith defense | Per-day exposure without a safe harbor punishes the companies that come forward. |
| Sec. 111(h). State attorneys general opt-in to receive reports and enforce | OPPOSE AS DRAFTED | Limit state enforcement to a backstop that follows federal interpretations, with notice to DOJ | One report routed to 50 possible enforcers is the patchwork re-entering through the back door. |
| Sec. 111(a)-(e). # Launch-day social posts (X and LinkedIn)

Work order ACIA-POL-2026-117. Five posts, each within 280 characters. Post 1 leads on X; posts 2-3 suit either platform; posts 4-5 suit LinkedIn. No member company may be named.

**Post 1 (X, lead)**

One national AI standard beats 50 state ones. Our new survey of 86 members: 61% say conflicting state definitions are their No. 1 compliance problem, and 1 in 3 startups delayed a launch in CA or NY this year. The Great American AI Act can fix this. #GAAIA

**Post 2 (X or LinkedIn)**

California, New York and Illinois now regulate frontier AI three different ways. Three definitions, three reporting clocks, three audit regimes. That is not safety. That is overhead. We need one clear federal standard. #GAAIA

**Post 3 (X or LinkedIn)**

Today ACIA filed comments on the Great American AI Act discussion draft. Our verdict: strong start. Make preemption permanent, narrow the incident definition, hold the 15-day reporting window, and keep CAISI voluntary. #AI

**Post 4 (LinkedIn)**

Speculative catastrophe scenarios are not a basis for law. Federal AI policy should regulate demonstrated harms, stay light-touch and risk-based, and keep the focus on costs and competitiveness. Our full GAAIA comments are out today.

**Post 5 (LinkedIn)**

15 days, not 72. California's incident reporting window gives developers time to establish facts and file an accurate report. We asked the bill's sponsors to hold that line. Cheap to say, expensive to get wrong.

**Character counts (post body only):** 256 | 225 | 222 | 233 | 211

# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on ACIA's GAAIA comments

Work order ACIA-POL-2026-117. Answers for Hill and committee staff, each under 120 words. Positions per messaging guide v3; survey data cited in aggregate only.

## 1. If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53. (Majority E&C staff)

We support one federal reporting channel. That is the point of preemption. Our objection is the definition in Sec. 101(7): it has no harm threshold, so any weight access, any risk-mitigation failure or any "loss of control" becomes a reportable federal incident, with penalties up to $1 million per day. A broad definition makes the federal regime heavier than the state rules it replaces. Our survey shows a median $310,000 to stand up a reporting function and 6.5 staff running parallel regimes today. Narrow the definition to actual or imminent material harm, keep the 15-day window, add confidentiality and a safe harbor, and we can support it.

## 2. Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept? (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned)

Plenty, and most are already in the draft. Our largest members already publish frontier AI frameworks under state law. ACIA accepts published frameworks with annual review (Sec. 111(a)); pre-deployment transparency reports (Sec. 111(c)); a single, narrow, confidential federal incident reporting channel on the draft's 15-day window (Secs. 111(f)-(g)); third-party verification retained by developers above $500 million in revenue (Sec. 112); and whistleblower anti-retaliation (Sec. 113). What we cannot accept: obligations keyed to speculative capability scenarios, a federal pre-deployment release gate, and 50-state enforcement through the attorney general opt-in (Sec. 111(h)). Regulate demonstrated harms, not hypothetical ones, and we are with you.

## 3. Three years or permanent: what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset? (Senate Commerce staff)

Permanent. Development is interstate commerce, and a three-year clock guarantees a relitigation in 2029 while telling compliance teams to budget for the patchwork's return. Our members are making five-year compute and facility commitments now. If a sunset is needed to move the bill, we would ask for three things: a longer runway; a clock that starts when the federal standard is fully operational, meaning regulations issued, the CAISI reporting mechanism live and verification organizations licensed; and no lapse before the standard has demonstrably replaced state obligations. We also oppose one-to-one preemption. Swapping one federal rule for one state rule is not a national standard.

## 4. CAISI is authorized at $100M per year. What's your view on the funding level? (Appropriations staff)

ACIA takes no position on the dollar figure. Our members care what the money buys. CAISI operates on roughly $15 million a year today, and the sponsors' own FAQ describes $100 million as an order-of-magnitude increase. A stably funded, codified CAISI is far preferable to 50 state analogues, so we are comfortable with the direction. Two guardrails: keep the mission voluntary, meaning guidelines, standards and evaluation by agreement with developers, with no mandatory pre-deployment testing authority; and watch the fee authority on verification organizations and large frontier developers, which passes costs straight back to industry. Whatever the number, annual reporting on what the center delivers would help appropriators judge it.
