DRAFT FOR PRESIDENT & CEO SIGN-OFF - Friday, Oct. 23, 2026
Work order ACIA-POL-2026-117. Internal header to be stripped before transmission.

---

[ACIA letterhead]

October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 on June 4, and for keeping it open for stakeholder comment ahead of introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington, D.C. coalition of roughly 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads in this technology.

ACIA supports the draft's central design. One clear federal standard, in place of a 50-state patchwork, is the most pro-innovation step Congress can take on AI. As we wrote in our March 2025 comments to the Office of Science and Technology Policy on the AI Action Plan, the patchwork is not an abstraction for our members. It is a line item, and it is growing.

We write with five requests. Make the draft's preemption of state AI development laws permanent. Narrow the definition of "critical safety incident." Hold the 15-day incident reporting window, and add confidentiality protections and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters. Keep the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) on a voluntary footing, with no mandatory pre-deployment testing authority. And hold every obligation in the final text to a demonstrated-harm test rather than to speculative risk scenarios.

## 1. One national standard (Sec. 121): support, and make it permanent

Section 121 would displace state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while leaving untouched state laws on use and deployment, laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. That is the right line. Development is interstate commerce. A model trained in one state is used in all 50, and it is built once, not 50 times.

The alternative is already here, and it is expensive. California's SB 53 has been in effect since Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, as amended in March 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 and puts critical safety incidents on a 72-hour clock. Illinois' SB 315, signed July 6, 2026 and effective Jan. 1, 2028, adds the country's first mandatory third-party audit requirement. Three states, three definitions, three reporting windows, three audit regimes. Colorado, meanwhile, repealed and replaced its own 2024 AI law in May 2026, weeks before it was to take effect and after a federal court had blocked its enforcement. Companies cannot plan against rules that change underneath them.

Our August 2026 survey of 86 responding members, aggregate data only and not a probability sample, puts numbers on this. Sixty-one percent of members rank conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem. Among startup members, 34 percent delayed a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Our largest developers report a median of 6.5 full-time employees to comply with California and New York in parallel, and a median of $1.4 million a year to maintain a published frontier safety framework. Those are resources not spent on training runs, chips or customers.

Our request on Sec. 121 is simple: make preemption permanent. If a sunset is unavoidable, it should not take effect until the federal standard is fully operational, regulations issued, the CAISI reporting mechanism live and independent verification organizations licensed, and it should be measured from that date, not from enactment. A three-year clock that starts at enactment guarantees a relitigation in 2029 and tells compliance teams to build for the patchwork's return. We would also caution against narrowing proposals, including the one-to-one preemption approach under discussion elsewhere in the framework. A preemption clause that swaps one federal rule for one state rule is not a national standard.

## 2. Incident reporting (Secs. 101(7), 111): opposed as drafted, fixable with five changes

ACIA supports a single federal incident reporting channel. We oppose the incident reporting provisions of Section 111 as drafted, for one reason above all: the definition is too broad to be workable.

Under Sec. 101(7), a "critical safety incident" is any unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights; any failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures; or any "loss of control" of the model. There is no harm threshold. On that definition, a routine security event, a guardrail that misfires during internal testing, or an anomaly that turns out to be nothing becomes a reportable federal incident, on a statute that carries civil penalties of up to $1 million per day. Our members' survey shows a median one-off cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident reporting function, before the first report is ever filed.

We ask the sponsors to make five changes.

First, narrow the definition in Sec. 101(7) to incidents that cause, or credibly threaten in the near term, actual and material harm to people, property or critical systems. A reporting regime should capture what went wrong, not what a hypothetical might one day go wrong.

Second, hold the 15-day reporting window in Sec. 111(g), with the 24-hour trigger for imminent risk of death or serious injury. Fifteen days matches California's SB 53. It is enough time for a developer to establish facts and file an accurate report, which is what regulators actually need. We note that the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, introduced in July and developed out of this framework, would tighten the clock to 72 hours, as New York does. We ask the sponsors to hold the line at 15 days and not import the 72-hour standard into the final text.

Third, make confidentiality explicit. The draft exempts from disclosure under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3) the information developers share with CAISI in connection with the center's evaluation functions. We ask that the same exemption and non-disclosure protections expressly cover incident reports submitted under Secs. 111(f) and 111(g), including any sharing with attorneys general under the opt-in provision in Sec. 111(h). Incident reports will contain some of the most security-sensitive information a developer holds. If a report can become a public document, or a discovery exhibit, developers will write it defensively, and the government will learn less.

Fourth, add a safe harbor for good-faith reports. A developer that reports promptly and honestly should not face penalties, or follow-on litigation, on the theory that its initial filing was incomplete. Safe harbors are what produce candid reporting.

Fifth, fix the enforcement back door. Under Sec. 111(h), state attorneys general may opt in to receive reports, and may then bring actions for civil penalties and injunctions. One incident, reported once to one federal official, could be routed to as many state enforcers as opt in, each with its own theory of the case. That is the patchwork re-entering the building through a side door. State enforcement, if retained at all, should be a backstop that follows federal interpretations, with notice to the Department of Justice.

## 3. CAISI (Sec. 102): support codification, keep the mission voluntary

ACIA supports Sec. 102. Codifying CAISI within the Department of Commerce, under a Secretary-appointed Director, with a mandate to develop voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards for AI security, to evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress, and to support synthetic content detection, is sound policy. Today CAISI operates on roughly $15 million a year. A codified, stably funded CAISI is a better answer than 50 state analogues, and we support the direction of the draft.

Two guardrails, please. First, the final text should state expressly that CAISI's testing and evaluation of frontier systems is voluntary and conducted by agreement with developers, as the center's existing cooperative arrangements with leading developers already work. Any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority, or any federal gate on releasing a model, would be the most consequential expansion of federal control over the AI stack in the final bill, and it would operate against speculative rather than demonstrated risk. We urge the sponsors to resist it in every title of the framework.

Second, take care with fee authority. Sec. 102 authorizes the center to collect fees from independent verification organizations and large frontier developers. Fees of that kind pass straight back to industry, and compliance costs fall hardest on startups and small suppliers even when they are nominally aimed at the largest firms. Scope them narrowly and give the Government Accountability Office a regular look.

ACIA takes no position on the $100 million annual authorization level for fiscal 2027 through 2029.

## 4. Regulate demonstrated harms, not speculative scenarios

The draft is built around "catastrophic risk," defined in Sec. 101 as a foreseeable and material risk of death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage. ACIA's members plan against real failure modes every day: weight theft, data center outages, supply chain interruptions, energy constraints. They do not plan against science fiction, and neither should federal law.

Speculative catastrophe scenarios are not a sound basis for legislation. They cannot be audited, they cannot be priced, and they invite agencies to regulate capability rather than harm. The draft's own structure shows the right instinct: a high threshold, tiered obligations, and the heaviest requirements reserved for developers above $500 million in revenue. We ask the sponsors to keep it that way, and to add a discipline to the definitional machinery: if CAISI or the Secretary recommends updating key definitions in future years, those changes should go through notice-and-comment and be subject to congressional review, not take effect as a matter of agency discretion. A light-touch, risk-based framework stays light-touch only if its thresholds do not drift.

## 5. Provisions ACIA supports

Our members strongly support the parts of the draft that expand capacity rather than paperwork, including the GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation, including energy (Sec. 122); the AI testbed program at the Energy Department, NIST and NSF (Sec. 401); the codification of the National AI Research Resource; grants to maintainers of critical open-source software (Sec. 311); the GAO review of model weight, data center and open-source security (Sec. 321); international standards coalitions that keep American firms at the head of the table (Sec. 411); reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 (Sec. 301); and penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials (Sec. 132). These are practical, bipartisan and overdue.

## Conclusion

This draft is the closest Congress has come to answering the question our members ask most often: which law applies? On the core choice, one national standard versus 50 state ones, ACIA is with you. Fix the incident reporting definition, protect the 15-day window, keep CAISI voluntary, and make preemption permanent, and the introduced bill will have our active support.

We would welcome the chance to walk through these comments with your staff and with the Energy and Commerce Committee, and to connect your offices with technical experts from our membership. Please contact our policy team at [ACIA policy contact: name, email, phone] to schedule.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
Washington, D.C.

**Who we are:** The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a Washington, D.C. coalition of about 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers behind U.S. AI leadership.

**Bottom line:** ACIA supports the discussion draft's central design. One clear federal standard beats a 50-state patchwork. We ask for five targeted changes before introduction.

## The problem: three states, three regimes

## Five asks

1. **Make preemption permanent (Sec. 121).** Development is interstate commerce. At minimum, no sunset until the federal standard is fully operational, measured from that date, not enactment. Reject one-to-one preemption, which swaps one federal rule for one state rule.

2. **Narrow "critical safety incident" (Sec. 101(7)).** As drafted it has no harm threshold: any weight access, any guardrail failure, any "loss of control" is reportable, with penalties up to $1 million per day. Limit it to incidents causing or credibly threatening actual and material harm.

3. **Hold the 15-day reporting window (Sec. 111(g)).** It matches California. Do not import New York's 72-hour clock. Add express confidentiality and a 552(b)(3) FOIA exemption for incident reports, and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters.

4. **Keep CAISI voluntary (Sec. 102).** Support codification. Testing and evaluation should be by agreement with developers. No mandatory pre-deployment testing authority and no federal release gate. Watch the fee authority on auditors and large developers.

5. **Close the state enforcement back door (Sec. 111(h)).** The attorney general opt-in lets one report be routed to any number of state enforcers. State enforcement, if retained, should be a backstop that follows federal interpretations.

# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on ACIA's GAAIA comments

Work order ACIA-POL-2026-117. Answers for Hill and committee staff, each under 120 words. Positions per messaging guide v3; survey data cited in aggregate only.

## 1. If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53. (Majority E&C staff)

We support one federal reporting channel. That is the point of preemption. Our objection is the definition in Sec. 101(7): it has no harm threshold, so any weight access, any risk-mitigation failure or any "loss of control" becomes a reportable federal incident, with penalties up to $1 million per day. A broad definition makes the federal regime heavier than the state rules it replaces. Our survey shows a median $310,000 to stand up a reporting function and 6.5 staff running parallel regimes today. Narrow the definition to actual or imminent material harm, keep the 15-day window, add confidentiality and a safe harbor, and we can support it.

## 2. Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept? (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned)

Plenty, and most are already in the draft. Our largest members already publish frontier AI frameworks under state law. ACIA accepts published frameworks with annual review (Sec. 111(a)); pre-deployment transparency reports (Sec. 111(c)); a single, narrow, confidential federal incident reporting channel on the draft's 15-day window (Secs. 111(f)-(g)); third-party verification retained by developers above $500 million in revenue (Sec. 112); and whistleblower anti-retaliation (Sec. 113). What we cannot accept: obligations keyed to speculative capability scenarios, a federal pre-deployment release gate, and 50-state enforcement through the attorney general opt-in (Sec. 111(h)). Regulate demonstrated harms, not hypothetical ones, and we are with you.

## 3. Three years or permanent: what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset? (Senate Commerce staff)

Permanent. Development is interstate commerce, and a three-year clock guarantees a relitigation in 2029 while telling compliance teams to budget for the patchwork's return. Our members are making five-year compute and facility commitments now. If a sunset is needed to move the bill, we would ask for three things: a longer runway; a clock that starts when the federal standard is fully operational, meaning regulations issued, the CAISI reporting mechanism live and verification organizations licensed; and no lapse before the standard has demonstrably replaced state obligations. We also oppose one-to-one preemption. Swapping one federal rule for one state rule is not a national standard.

## 4. CAISI is authorized at $100M per year. What's your view on the funding level? (Appropriations staff)

ACIA takes no position on the dollar figure. Our members care what the money buys. CAISI operates on roughly $15 million a year today, and the sponsors' own FAQ describes $100 million as an order-of-magnitude increase. A stably funded, codified CAISI is far preferable to 50 state analogues, so we are comfortable with the direction. Two guardrails: keep the mission voluntary, meaning guidelines, standards and evaluation by agreement with developers, with no mandatory pre-deployment testing authority; and watch the fee authority on verification organizations and large frontier developers, which passes costs straight back to industry. Whatever the number, annual reporting on what the center delivers would help appropriators judge it.
